The far side has never been fully looted, and the reason is printed on every casing. The paint sticks mark the skip pattern. Walk it. Do not test the parts they do not mark.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: Each step is placed with the toe first, testing before the weight commits. The tarmac is hot under the sun and the heat makes the casings tick, a sound like a clock in every direction. The marking paint fades in a season and the repainting is the work of people who cross this ground regularly enough to know which casings have shifted in the rain. You follow their paint. You do not trust your own feet.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The lower levels flooded first and the waterline is visible on the facade, a dark stain that climbs past the third floor. The dry upper floors are a museum of bad luck: a vinyl collection with the sleeves still dated, gold bars in a vault door left open, epoxy resin in drums that never got used because the leak was already in. Everything here was chosen for comfort. Nothing here was chosen for survival. The water laps at the third floor and has not risen in a year, which is either good news or a pause.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The vault door is open and the gold bars are still inside, stacked on shelves with the price tags attached. The tags are in a currency that no longer exists. Beside the gold, a shelf holds a set of crystal glassware, each glass in its velvet slot, none of them broken. The glass is worth more than the gold now, because the glass can carry water and the gold cannot. Someone has taken one glass. The velvet slot is empty and the dust around it shows the outline of the glass that was there.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The water in the Odeon has settled at the level of row F, and the screen is intact, the last thing in the building still facing its audience. The seats below the waterline are folded down by people who sat in them. The film in the projector is still wound on its reel. The screen has not changed its image in three years: it is grey, and it is what everyone came to see. The balcony stays dry and the balcony is where you stand to look at the screen that is not playing.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The projection booth has a chair with a cushion and the cushion has a shape. The projector has been maintained: the lens is clean, the gate is oiled, the film path is threaded and ready. The booth has a window that looks down at the screen, and the window is clean on the inside. Someone has been sitting here, watching a screen that shows nothing, in a room that was built for stories. The projector could still run. The film is still on the reel. The audience is in the water below.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The long table was salvaged from the municipal offices and the chairs do not match. The whiteboards on the wall still hold the last pre-war agenda in one marker color, and new items have been added in three others: water rations, duty roster, radiation count. The markers are in a cup on the table and the cup has been refilled from a kit that is almost empty. The room is the closest thing the shelter has to neutral ground, and the neutral ground is a table that was not built for this.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The whiteboard for water rations has been erased and rewritten so many times the surface is stained grey with marker residue. The numbers change but the argument does not, and the argument is always about the same thing: who gets how much of what, and for how long. The chair nearest the water board has armrests worn smooth from hands gripping them during meetings. The meetings are held every three days. The meetings have not been missed.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The fluorescent tubes hum even when the main power is offline, drawing from a circuit that nobody has traced to its source. The cabinet of scavenged supplies is organised by type and by expiry, and the expiry dates are written in pencil so they can be updated. A dosage ledger on the counter has more entries every week. The curtain dividing treatment from triage is more psychological than practical, but it is clean, and the cleaning is the point.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The infirmary smells of antiseptic and burnt coffee, and the two smells have merged into something that is the smell of the shelter's attempt to keep its people alive. The antiseptic is diluted, stretched, rationed by the drop. The coffee is instant and has been instant for three years and the tin it comes in has a label that has been hand-updated with each refill. The examination couches have paper rolls that are changed weekly. The paper is not medical grade. The couches are.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The electrified fence hums at a frequency that makes the hair on your arms stand up before you reach it. Beyond the fence, containers are stacked in rows and the rows form streets, and the streets have names chalked on the container sides. The market smells of solder and hot plastic. A factor's stall near the entrance has copper wire wound on spools sorted by gauge, and the sorting is meticulous. The chips on the next shelf are tested and labelled with their voltage tolerance.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The workbench at the back of the market has a magnifying glass on an articulated arm and the arm has been tightened so many times the joints are stiff with solder drips. The bench surface is scarred with cut marks and burn marks and the marks are layered, the newest on top of the oldest, a geological record of things being taken apart and put back together. A half-repaired radio sits on the bench, its case open, its internals exposed like organs. The repair is careful. The repair will be finished today or tomorrow, depending on whether the part arrives.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The rail cars have been converted into dwellings and workshops, and the conversion is permanent: welding beads run along every seam, the doors have been cut and rehinged, and the roofs are buried under a layer of railroad ballast that insulates against the cold. The forges are banked but warm, and the sound of hammering comes from inside the cars at irregular intervals. The air smells of hot iron and coal dust. The town is built from the thing that brought it here, and the thing that brought it here was a train that stopped.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The forge in car number seven has an anvil that was cut from a rail section, and the rail section still has the manufacturer's stamp on it. The hammer is shaped from a bolt the diameter of a wrist, and the handle is wrapped in leather that has been oiled and re-oiled until it is dark with the work. The work gang forges high-tensile hardware: bolts, brackets, hinges, the small metal things that hold the world together when the world has come apart. The forge is the heart of the town and the heart beats in iron.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The transmitter mast is wired into a parking structure's stairwell, the antenna run up through a gap in the collapsed roof and guyed to rebar that was never meant to hold a mast. Nobody broadcasts from here more than once; the signal gets relayed onward from a different stairwell the next week. The log taped inside the door lists only call times, never names, in more handwriting styles than any one broadcaster could produce alone. Eighteen rads an hour, chosen for exactly that reason.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation

environmental_texts.text: The transmitter key is a telegraph paddle modified with a microswitch, and the paddle has been worn smooth on the contact by three years of different hands sending different messages from different stairwells. The signal goes out and the signal is relayed and the signal cannot be traced because the trace would have to follow it through a dozen stairwells and a dozen different broadcasters who do not know each other and will never meet. The Understory is a voice that has no mouth. The voice says: you are not alone.
environmental_texts.author: narrator_observation
